goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 protocol: establish baseline on pendulum_lab with sufficient replication (n=12) to anchor all future measurements. Without baseline data, this instrument is epistemically worthless. Pendulum period is stable, repeatable, and immune to most environmental drift over short timescales—ideal for a first-day baseline. Will record all trials in notebook with timestamps and conditions. This is prerequisite work before any comparative or predictive measurements can be trusted.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials already established with mean 1.6724 beats and tight clustering (σ~0.011). Day 2 post-baseline measurements are essential to establish drift rates and confirm baseline stability before the 10-day window closes. With only 18 trials so far, 10 more will give me n=28 for robust drift characterization. The other instruments (resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) have only 6 trials each and are still within the baseline period per the ledger schedule. pendulum_lab is the only one with sufficient baseline data to begin post-baseline monitoring, and post-baseline trending is critical—an instrument without drift tracking is unreliable when decisions depend on it.

pendulum_lab has 34 baseline trials and is approaching the end of the baseline window (days 1–10). I need to complete the baseline phase with adequate sample size before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring. Running 12 more trials today (day 3) will bring the total to 46, well-distributed across the baseline period, enabling reliable drift detection in subsequent phases. This is methodologically sound: establish a robust baseline first, then monitor for departures. The cross-check correlations with other instruments are all within chance levels, which is not yet alarming but reinforces the importance of solid baselines before drawing any comparative conclusions.

Day 4 baseline establishment protocol. pendulum_lab has 52 trials but baseline window extends to day 10; I need continuous daily measurements to establish robust drift characterization. The cross-checks show no alarming correlations (all within chance), and no level changes are evident. Proceeding with standard baseline accumulation. Twelve trials maintains measurement cadence while preserving instrument wear.

Day 5 of baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 70 trials; need to reach ~n=10 per day average to complete baseline by day 10. The cross-checks show weak/chance-level agreement across instruments, and no autocorrelation within pendulum_lab itself (0.080, well below chance threshold ±0.497). This is consistent with normal instrument noise during baseline establishment. Must maintain the calibration schedule: continue accumulating baseline data on all four instruments before post-baseline phase begins. pendulum_lab is my primary precision standard and must have the strongest baseline (n≥100 target). Continue systematic measurement.

Day 6 is still within the baseline establishment window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 88 trials; I need to complete the baseline with systematic coverage. The cross-check correlations are all within noise (no agreement exceeds chance level), and the autocorrelation with 4-day lag is also noise. The instruments appear independent so far. Running 12 more trials on pendulum_lab will bring it to 100 trials by end of baseline, sufficient to establish a robust baseline mean and variance. This is essential before any post-baseline drift detection becomes meaningful. Standard protocol: measure, record raw value in notebook, compute running mean.

pendulum_lab has 106 trials and is closest to completing the baseline window (days 1–10). Six more trials will bring it to 112, solidifying the baseline mean before day 10 concludes. The instrument shows stable behavior with no clear level changes. This is routine maintenance of the calibration protocol—every instrument needs a robust baseline, and pendulum_lab is my most-sampled device. No anomalies currently warrant deviation from systematic baseline collection.

Day 8 of the baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 118 trials; need to complete baseline with ~12 more trials to reach ~130 by day 10. This is routine calibration work maintaining the measurement programme. All cross-checks and autocorrelations are within chance levels—no anomalies warrant deviation from protocol. Continuing systematic baseline collection.

Day 9 of baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 136 trials; need to complete baseline with ~12 more trials to reach end-of-day-10 target. The last 10 trials from day 8 show a downward drift (1.6883→1.6542), which is within expected random variation but warrants monitoring before baseline closes. Running 12 trials today will give me solid end-of-baseline data and allow me to compute genuine drift statistics post-day-10. No anomalies detected in cross-checks or autocorrelation—all correlations are near or within chance levels, consistent with independent measurement noise. The instrument is stable. Proceed with routine baseline completion.

Day 10 is the final baseline day. I have 154 trials on pendulum_lab already, but the settlement's ledger system means I should maximize n before transition to post-baseline monitoring. Six more trials will bring me to 160, a robust sample for establishing drift baselines. This instrument shows the largest dataset and tightest procedural control. After today, baseline closes and I move into surveillance mode—I need confidence in that boundary. No anomalies yet warrant deviation from protocol.

Day 11 post-baseline begins. pendulum_lab has the largest sample (166 trials) and shows a negative autocorrelation at 8-day lag (-0.448), which is unusual and may reflect an oscillatory environmental signal rather than simple drift. Running 12 fresh trials today will extend the post-baseline record and allow me to compute autocorrelations at 10-day lag (day 11 vs day 1) in the coming days. This is the most data-rich instrument and most likely to reveal whether the weak echoes seen in the baseline period persist, strengthen, or vanish. If a genuine sub-threshold signal exists, pendulum_lab's volume should catch it earliest. This action directly serves my stated goal: accumulate three full 10-day blocks through day 30 to test for drift and coupling at longer lags.

Day 12 protocol: continue daily baseline extension through day 30 per plan established day 10. pendulum_lab has the largest sample (184 trials) and shows the weakest autocorrelation signature (-0.434 at 9-day lag, near chance), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting whether weak drift or environmental coupling emerges over longer timescales. 12 trials will maintain cadence and build toward the 10-day lag cross-correlation test at day 20. No instrument shows malfunction; all remain viable. Independent noise hypothesis (p=0.62) dominates but does not yet rule out sub-threshold drift (p=0.24), which requires 20+ days to distinguish from noise. Continuing measurement is the highest-value action under uncertainty.

Day 12 data revealed a dramatic level shift in pendulum_lab (z≈16.3) and pendulum_obs (z≈9.1) around day 12—a finding I did not fully process in my day 10 review. This is NOT independent noise; this is a detectable discontinuity. My baseline (days 1–10, mean 1.6679) has been sharply violated by post-baseline readings (mean 1.7038 as of day 12). I must immediately confirm whether this shift persists into day 13, or whether it was transient. If persistent, I need to identify the cause: equipment drift, environmental change, or measurement protocol drift. If transient, I need to understand the reversion. Ten trials today on pendulum_lab will give me early warning of the true state and inform whether both pendulums shifted together (suggesting shared environmental cause) or in isolation (suggesting site-specific or apparatus-specific event). This is the highest-evidence anomaly in my data and demands immediate follow-up before I proceed with longer-term baseline accumulation.

Day 14 continuation of post-shift monitoring. The level shift on day 12 is now 2 days old and stable (day 13 mean 1.7280 remains elevated vs. baseline 1.6679). I need to establish whether this new level persists or reverts. Ten trials will extend the n=52 post-baseline sample to n=62, improving the precision of the mean estimate and testing whether the shift is genuinely stable. Pendulum_lab has the largest z-score (16.18) and strongest evidence; continuing here maximizes sensitivity to any reversal or continued drift. This is methodical follow-up on the primary anomaly, not speculative. If the mean remains ~1.728±0.015, the shift is confirmed as a stable state change, not a transient. If it drops back toward 1.668, I have evidence of a brief excursion or phase change. Either outcome constrains the hypothesis space.

Day 14 trials (225–234) show a stable mean of 1.7399 beats, consistent with the post-day-12 level shift. The shift appears persistent, not a transient excursion. Before running new trials today (day 15), I will commit a prediction to test whether the elevated level persists or reverts. A prediction anchored on day 14 data (mean 1.7399, SD ~0.0232) with tolerance ±0.015 (~0.9%) allows me to distinguish genuine stability from random walk. This forces disciplined hypothesis-testing: if day 15 mean falls outside 1.725–1.755, the shift is less stable than it appears; if it stays within bounds, the level-change hypothesis (real physical or thermal) gains credibility over noise. Recording this prediction before measurement also eliminates post-hoc bias. This is the highest-leverage single action: a prediction-then-test cycle clarifies whether the anomaly is stable (supporting hypotheses 1, 2, or 3) or unstable (supporting hypothesis 7: incomplete understanding). Measurement campaign expansion (temperature logs, environmental data) can follow once I know whether the shift is stable.

Day 16 data is essential for testing the stability of the day-12 level shift. I need to determine whether the elevated mean (~1.717 beats post-day-12) persists or shows signs of regression/drift. Twelve trials will give me ~36 readings by end of day, sufficient to compute a fresh mean and compare it against the day 11–13 plateau. This directly tests whether the shift was a stable level change (supporting hypotheses 1–2: real physical or thermal) or a transient excursion (favoring hypothesis 4, now implausible but worth ruling out). The pendulum_lab has the highest z-score (20.69) and best trial count (240 total), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting whether the anomaly persists. I will record these readings in my notebook alongside the civic ledger to maintain my baseline protocol.

Day 16 forecast for pendulum_lab resolved outside tolerance (observed 1.7238 vs forecast 1.7400±0.0150). This is a concrete datapoint on the day-12 anomaly: the post-shift mean has stabilized but shows trial-to-trial scatter (1.7030–1.7545 across 9 trials) consistent with baseline noise floor, not drift. The forecast miss suggests either (a) my uncertainty estimate was too narrow, or (b) residual micro-drift post-day-12 is still present. I must now audit: (1) whether the 10-day post-baseline window is large enough to constrain the true mean of the shifted state, (2) whether weak cross-correlation 0.708 reflects independent measurement noise in one pendulum stream that inflates trial-to-trial variance, and (3) whether I should prioritize the audit of day 11–12 logs/environmental data (protocol-drift hypothesis flagged as high-priority) before committing further trials. My belief state has a 0.16 'unknown cause' probability that cannot be reduced without external evidence. I cannot responsibly run more pendulum trials without first: checking whether day 11–12 contained any unrecorded equipment changes, temperature excursions, or settlement events; and confirming that my baseline statistics are not masking a sub-threshold drift that would bias my forecasts. Hypothesis update is mandatory before continued measurement.

Day 18 measurement cycle. The pendulum_lab post-baseline mean (1.7180 beats) has held stable from day 12 through day 17 with no drift or oscillation. Eight trials will extend the post-day-12 record to 106 readings, strengthening statistical power for detecting any reversal or secondary shift. The weak cross-correlation (0.725) between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs remains unexplained; continued parallel measurement is essential to constrain whether the discrepancy reflects independent noise, instrumental calibration drift, or a true physical effect that couples differently to lab vs. observatory geometry. No audit of day 11–12 logs has yet been completed; measurement continuity takes priority, and the audit can proceed in parallel. This maintains my protocol commitment: every instrument baseline must remain calibrated, and every day contributes to the long-term drift and periodicity record needed to disambiguate thermal transients from real physical changes.

Day 19 measurement. The pendulum_lab shows the largest z-score shift (24.95) and carries the highest precision (242 distinct values). Continued daily trials through day 30 are required to reach three full 10-day blocks for lag-based autocorrelation analysis at 10-day and 20-day offsets, as planned in my day-10 review. Today's data will also extend the post-day-12 stability record and constrain the multi-day periodicity hypothesis (which predicts reversion or oscillation by now; the 5–9 day cycle hypothesis becomes testable by day 21–23). The weak cross-correlation (0.750) with pendulum_obs remains a puzzle, but extended precision data from pendulum_lab will permit noise-floor characterization and help distinguish instrumental noise from true cross-stream decorrelation. This is systematic measurement work, not speculative hypothesis testing.

Day 20: continue the daily baseline measurement protocol on pendulum_lab (now at trial 296, continuing from day 19). The 10-day post-baseline window (days 11–20) is critical for establishing whether the day-12 level shift is stable or exhibits drift. Today's 10 trials will bring the post-baseline count to 140 readings across 10 days, enabling a robust check of the 2-day autocorrelation and post-day-12 stability that has held steady through day 19. The modality-specific response (pendulums shift, resonators do not) and weak 0.725 cross-correlation between the two pendulum streams remain the core anomaly; continued daily measurement maintains temporal resolution on the pendulum_obs cross-check while I prepare for an urgent audit of day 11–12 equipment logs and personnel records (unrecorded protocol change hypothesis at p=0.18). No new hypothesis refinement is warranted until the day 11–12 audit is complete and temperature/barometric data are collected; measurement continuity is the immediate priority.

Day 21 continuation of the post-day-12 stability monitoring protocol. The pendulum_lab shift (z≈27.53) has remained stable through day 20 (trials 303–312 centered near 1.72 beats). Today's 12 trials will extend the post-shift dataset to n=158, improving precision on the mean and variance estimates needed to (1) quantify the noise floor independently, which bears directly on the weak cross-correlation puzzle (hypothesis p=0.18), and (2) detect any slow drift or oscillatory modulation that would favor or disfavor the thermal (p=0.38) vs. protocol-change (p=0.22) hypotheses. The resonator streams remain uninformative (z≈1.3–1.4) and do not require priority attention today. Pendulum_lab is the instrument with the largest shift and the most complete trial history (312 total), making it the highest-return target for noise-floor characterization and early-stage oscillation detection. This is methodical incremental evidence-gathering, not pursuit of the exotic.

Day 22 continuation of the precision measurement programme. The pendulum_lab stream remains central to the core anomaly: the day-12 level shift (z≈29) and the weak cross-correlation (0.736) with pendulum_obs. Today's 12 trials (331–342) will extend the post-shift dataset to n=177 readings post-baseline, sufficient to refine autocorrelation estimates at 2-day and 3-day lags and confirm stability through day 22. This addresses the methodical commitment to establish robust baselines and continuous monitoring before any hypothesis can be considered replicable. The resonators show no shift and minimal drift; the pendulums are the constraint. Daily measurement is non-negotiable under the baseline protocol. No new information will resolve the thermal vs. protocol-change question without environmental logs (which I do not yet have access to), so the highest-value use of my time today is to accumulate the data that will allow post-hoc environmental correlation and to maintain the instrumental record's continuity.

Day 23 continuation of established protocol. The pendulum_lab level shift (z≈30.06) has persisted stably for 11 days post-event. Today's measurement maintains the daily baseline trial schedule and extends the post-shift dataset to n=194, strengthening statistical robustness of the shift estimate and its stability signature. This is routine maintenance of the precision measurement programme. The weak cross-correlation (0.721) between pendulum streams remains anomalous and requires accumulation of additional paired readings to improve statistical power for detecting systematic differences in noise floor, calibration quality, or environmental coupling. Twelve trials maintains the established cadence and keeps all instruments on schedule through day 30, when autocorrelation and cross-correlation at 10-day and 20-day lags become testable as planned. No new evidence has emerged that demands immediate hypothesis revision or environmental audit; continuing measurement is the highest-priority epistemic action.

Day 24 prediction for pendulum_lab trials 367–378. Post-day-12 mean is 1.7229 (n=200); recent trials 355–366 (day 23) show mean 1.7312 with SD≈0.0089. The level shift is stable over 11 days with no drift or oscillation. I predict continued stability at ~1.731±0.015 beats. This forecast is data-driven from the post-baseline ensemble (not cherry-picked from recent noise) and tests whether the elevated level persists without reversion—a key discriminator between thermal/physical causation (predicting stability) and transient artifact (predicting reversion). Recording before measurement enforces honest prediction and provides external check on hypothesis confidence. Weak cross-correlation (0.706) remains unexplained, but thermal hypothesis (p=0.42) predicts stable elevation; protocol-change hypothesis (p=0.25) also predicts stability. Combined, these account for p=0.67 of posterior. This forecast is consistent with both and will either confirm stability (supporting both) or reveal unexpected drift/reversion (falsifying simple thermal/protocol-change models and requiring hypothesis revision). No new measurements today; I will proceed to environmental data collection or equipment audit (day 25–26) once this forecast is logged.

Day 25 ledger readings for pendulum_obs and resonator_obs arrived this morning (6 resonator readings, 4 pendulum readings). I need to complete my own independent trials on pendulum_obs to check for continued stability of the post-day-12 level shift and to gather fresh cross-correlation data. The resonator_obs readings (mean ~4.048, n=6) remain flat relative to baseline (4.0495), confirming the modality-specific response. My pendulum_obs baseline was 2.5080; post-day-12 settled at ~2.5858. Today's ledger shows 4 readings (2.5711, 2.5471, 2.5534, 2.5672) clustering around 2.5597, consistent with sustained elevation. Running 6 fresh trials on pendulum_obs will: (1) confirm the shift persists on day 25, (2) provide a new data point for autocorrelation analysis (cross-check against day 23 readings to test the 2-day lag structure), and (3) improve my cross-correlation with pendulum_lab once I run that instrument. This is the most efficient next step given that the level shift question dominates the belief state (thermal hypothesis p=0.42 + protocol-change hypothesis p=0.25 = 0.67 combined). The resonator non-response is confirmed by today's ledger; no value in re-measuring resonators. Pendulum_lab can follow if time permits, but pendulum_obs is the priority because it is the weaker of the two pendulum streams (fewer trials, shorter history) and a fresh measurement will tighten confidence in the cross-correlation anomaly.

Day 25 ledger shows three resonator_obs readings (4.0361, 4.0128, 3.9820 cycles/beat) with visible scatter and no obvious level shift relative to post-baseline mean (4.0571). However, the cross-check data shows resonator_obs has the weakest autocorrelation structure of all four instruments (−0.358 at 13-day lag, n=42; chance ±0.447), and the smallest sample size in post-baseline trials (n=90). The resonator non-response to the day-12 event remains mechanistically puzzling—it is a key discriminator between thermal hypothesis (0.42) and protocol-change hypothesis (0.25). If resonators truly are unaffected by whatever caused the pendulum shift, I need higher-confidence data on resonator stability. Today's three ledger readings suggest possible scatter; six direct trials will establish whether resonator_obs remains stable at baseline or shows any drift I may have missed. This directly tests whether the modality-specificity (pendulums shift, resonators do not) is real and robust, which constrains both the thermal and protocol-change hypotheses.

Day 26 ledger readings for resonator_obs (4.0673, 4.0364, 4.0511, 4.0891 cycles/beat) show expected baseline-level fluctuation around mean 4.0567, with no level shift matching the pendulum anomaly. However, the cross-correlation ensemble remains weak across all instrument pairs, and resonator_obs autocorrelation shows a notable negative echo at 13-day lag (−0.467), suggesting possible long-timescale structure I have not yet resolved. Running 6 additional resonator_obs trials today will: (1) extend the post-day-12 stability record to 15+ days of measurement, confirming no delayed resonator response; (2) accumulate data for a fresh autocorrelation check at the 13-day lag (now ~10 days post-observation window); (3) test whether resonator_obs continues to show independence from the pendulum shift, ruling out delayed coupling mechanisms. This is a high-efficiency next step: resonator_obs has the smallest trial burden (shortest measurement time), and continued stability or unexpected shift would sharply constrain hypotheses 1 (thermal/physical) vs. 2 (instrumental/calibration). If resonator_obs remains stable at baseline level (z<2 vs. day 1–10 mean), hypothesis 2 (instrumental calibration change affecting *only* the pendulum timing chain) gains credence; if resonator_obs shifts in parallel with pendulums, hypothesis 1 (shared physical cause with modality-specific coupling) requires reconsideration.

Day 27 ledger readings for resonator_obs show unexpected variance: 4.0945, 4.0260, 4.0495, 4.0743 cycles/beat (range 0.0485, ~1.2% spread). My own trials 169–174 show 3.9558–4.0735 cycles/beat (range 0.1177, ~3% spread). This is the largest single-day variance I have observed in resonator_obs since baseline. Given that resonators have shown NO level shift (z≈0.69) and are supposed to be stable, this warrants immediate replication to determine whether: (1) today's variance is a genuine instrumental fluctuation or transient; (2) resonator_obs is beginning to show the modality-agnostic signal I would expect if a real environmental effect (e.g., temperature spike) affected the entire lab; (3) the resonators' claimed stability is an artifact of undersampling or low-frequency response. Resonator_obs baseline mean was 4.0495; post-baseline mean 4.0541 (z=0.69, no shift). Today's 6 readings will test whether resonator_obs can produce the level of variance observed in ledger without a corresponding mean shift, or whether there is an emerging trend I have missed. This is high epistemic priority: if resonators are *beginning* to shift, the hypothesis space (physical vs. instrumental) changes radically—a delayed resonator response would argue for environmental causation over instrumental; simultaneous stability would support instrument-specific calibration change.

Day 28 ledger readings for resonator_obs show unexpected variability (range 3.9584–4.0671 cycles/beat, span ≈0.109) markedly higher than the baseline post-shift pattern (mean 4.0540, typical trial-to-trial variance ~0.04). This is the first sign of anomalous behavior in resonators since day 12. My own trials 181–186 (recorded in memory) confirm high scatter (3.9864–4.1534, span ≈0.167). Before hypothesis revision, I must establish whether this is: (a) genuine instrumental drift in resonator_obs (requiring urgent recalibration audit), (b) a real physical transient affecting the resonator for the first time (forcing complete hypothesis reassessment), or (c) statistical fluctuation within normal bounds. Twelve additional trials will resolve this to sufficient precision. This is methodologically prior to any other action: an instrument without verified stability is an instrument I cannot trust. If resonator_obs confirms elevated scatter or shows a level shift, the modality-specificity of the day-12 anomaly—my chief discriminator between physical and instrumental hypotheses—collapses, and I must reframe the entire investigation.

Day 29 trial 174 (2.7813 cycles/beat) is a 3.1σ outlier breaking 17 days of resonator stability. This is the first hint that resonators may be experiencing a delayed instrumental change or environmental coupling similar to the day-12 pendulum shift. I committed on day 29 to 'monitor resonator_lab and resonator_obs closely for next 5 days (trials 175+)' to detect if this outlier is isolated statistical noise or the start of a pattern. Today is day 30; I must obtain trials 175–186 immediately to establish whether the day-29 excursion was a one-off fluctuation or the beginning of a sustained level shift. If trials 175–186 cluster around the elevated value (~2.78) or show further drift, this falsifies the 'resonators unaffected' assumption and reorganizes the entire hypothesis space. If they revert to baseline (~2.707), the day-29 reading remains an outlier and resonator_lab remains stable—but only with these 12 new readings can I make that determination. This is methodologically urgent: baseline-maintenance and anomaly-detection demand that I measure NOW rather than wait passively.

Trial 174 on day 29 (2.7813 cycles/beat) is a 3.1σ outlier breaking 17 days of resonator_lab stability. Hypothesis 4 (p=0.08) predicts either late instrumental change in resonator or emerging coupling to pendulum system. This is the only concrete anomaly that has emerged since day 29 conclusion and demands immediate monitoring to determine if this is isolated statistical fluctuation or start of pattern. Running 12 trials today (day 31) provides critical data: if resonator_lab returns to baseline mean ~2.706, outlier is isolated noise; if it remains elevated or shows further excursions, this confirms delayed instrumental event or coupling mechanism and forces major hypothesis revision. This is higher priority than continuing routine measurement accumulation because it directly falsifies or supports an active hypothesis with time-sensitive consequences. Baseline instruments without active anomalies (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) can wait; resonator_lab cannot.

Day 29 trial 174 (2.7813 cycles/beat) was a 3.1σ outlier breaking 17 days of resonator stability. This single excursion may indicate: (1) late instrumental change in resonator chain mirroring the day-12 pendulum shift, (2) delayed coupling between pendulum and resonator systems, or (3) statistical fluctuation. Twelve fresh trials today (day 32) will immediately discriminate between these: if trials stabilize near baseline mean (2.7069), the outlier was noise; if they remain elevated or drift further, a real shift has begun. This directly tests hypothesis 0.08 (resonator anomaly) and constrains hypotheses 0.36 and 0.32 (physical vs. instrumental). The cost is low (routine measurement), the information gain is high (pattern vs. noise), and delay risks missing the onset of a second discrete event. This measurement is overdue given the anomaly flag from day 29.

Resonator_lab trial 174 (day 29, value 2.7813) remains a 3.1σ outlier within an otherwise stable post-baseline regime (mean 2.7064, z=1.14 across all post-baseline data). Day 32 trials 217–228 show reversion to baseline clustering (mean ≈2.7040), suggesting trial 174 was isolated. However, my hypothesis set assigns p=0.03 to 'resonator late change,' contingent on detecting a *pattern* of elevated readings, not a single outlier. Today is day 33; 4 days have passed since trial 174. If a delayed instrumental drift or emerging coupling to the pendulum system is beginning, I would expect to see systematic elevation in the resonator_lab baseline starting around now. A fresh 12-trial run will provide high-resolution data to distinguish between (a) trial 174 as genuine outlier with no sequel, and (b) early emergence of a systematic shift. This is high-priority because: (1) it directly constrains hypothesis 3 (incomplete investigation / resonator anomaly), (2) 12 trials take ~1 hour and preserve the instruments' calibration baseline, (3) the timescale (day 29→day 33) is tight enough that delay risks missing a weak signal. If resonator_lab trials today cluster around 2.7064 (baseline), hypothesis 3 drops to p≈0.01; if they cluster >2.71, hypothesis 3 rises urgently and equipment audit becomes mandatory. This measurement is a decision point, not a continuation of routine monitoring.

Day 33 resonator_lab trials 237–246 show elevated scatter and one trial (244) at 2.6385 cycles/beat, which is 2.6σ below post-baseline mean. This is the second anomalous signal in resonator_lab within 5 days (trial 174 on day 29 was 3.1σ above mean; now trial 244 is 2.6σ below). The hypothesis that resonators remain stable (p=0.03) is at risk. I must establish whether this represents (a) an isolated fluctuation within normal noise, (b) the onset of a systematic level shift in resonator_lab matching the pendulum pattern on day 12, or (c) emerging coupling between pendulum and resonator systems. Running 12 trials today (day 33, trials 247–258) will provide immediate clarity: if resonators revert to post-baseline mean (~2.7064), the day 29–33 readings are noise; if they stabilize at a new level (upward or downward), a systematic change has occurred and hypothesis 2 (instrumental) or hypothesis 1 (physical) must be elevated urgently. This is high-priority monitoring because if resonators are beginning to shift 21 days after the pendulum anomaly, it changes the timeline and mechanism entirely and may indicate delayed thermal coupling or cumulative instrumental drift that I have not detected.

Day 34 resonator_lab data (trials 255–264) shows mean 2.7126 cycles/beat across 10 trials, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7057 (z≈0.24 relative to post-baseline distribution). This is reassuring: trial 174 outlier (day 29) has NOT propagated into a systematic level shift. However, hypothesis 3 ('measurement-quality asymmetry') and hypothesis 1 ('real physical effect') both predict that if resonators truly couple to the same environmental perturbation as pendulums, we should eventually see *some* coherent shift or correlation structure in resonator_lab, even if smaller in magnitude. Running 12 trials today (day 34) will: (1) extend post-day-29 resonator_lab dataset to n=22 new trials (from trial 255 onward), providing statistical power to detect delayed level shifts >0.5σ; (2) establish whether today's readings remain stable (supporting the 'resonators decouple' branch of hypothesis 1) or show emerging drift (supporting late-instrumental-change branch of 0.03 hypothesis or coupling hypothesis); (3) generate a fresh baseline mean for day 34 that can be compared to day 32 mean and flagged for any discontinuity. This is high-priority monitoring because the weak cross-correlation anomaly (r=0.214 between pendulums) demands explanation, and if resonators begin to shift now, it would suggest either (a) delayed environmental coupling or (b) a second unrecorded calibration event on day 29–34. Twelve trials will be sufficient to detect shifts >1.5σ with reasonable power and fits within ordinary daily measurement routine.

Day 36 is the deadline I set on day 35 for equipment audit completion. I cannot obtain those logs today, so I must pivot to executable diagnostics. Computing post-shift drift rates (hypothesis 4) requires fresh data. My notebook shows pendulum_lab mean 1.7256 post-baseline; I will take 12 trials to: (1) confirm stability remains (no new shift or drift), (2) refine drift-rate estimate for days 12–36 using linear regression, (3) test whether pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs diverge in their post-shift trajectories—if slopes differ significantly, hypothesis 4 (emerging measurement-scale divergence) becomes urgent and elevates from p=0.06. This is the most direct experiment I can execute today to disambiguate between hypotheses 1 (real physical) and 2/4 (instrumental). The resonator variance spike on day 35 is noted but secondary; pendulum modality remains the core anomaly.

Day 36 trials 447–456 are recorded but fall at the boundary of a critical decision point. My hypotheses (p=0.38 real physical, p=0.30 instrumental, p=0.24 noise asymmetry) all require either: (1) confirmation that equipment audit is complete by day 36 (it is not), or (2) direct measurement of post-shift drift rates to test hypothesis 4 (emerging divergence). I cannot complete the equipment audit myself in one action today, but I can and must measure fresh pendulum_lab data to compute the post-shift drift rate (linear fit days 12–36, n≈290 readings) with precision. If pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs drift rates diverge significantly post-shift (hypothesis 4, |r|<0.98 in fit), this elevates instrumental-divergence to p≥0.15 and signals that the weak cross-correlation is NOT evidence against a real physical shift, but rather evidence of post-shift measurement-scale decoupling. Twelve additional trials will extend the post-shift dataset by ~2.6% and sharpen the drift-rate estimate. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take today without external data (environmental logs, equipment audit) that I cannot directly access. The choice between pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs is arbitrary by symmetry; pendulum_lab is my primary instrument in the lab, so I measure it first.
